lessons.t: HTML Base — Tags, Headings, Links, Images, Lists
lessons.sub: The skeleton of every web page
lessons.goal: By the end you can write a valid HTML page from scratch using headings, paragraphs, links, images and lists, and explain what the browser does with each tag.
lessons.body:
1. HTML is structure, not looks

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes what things are, not how they look. A heading is a heading, a paragraph is a paragraph, and a link is a link. Colour and layout belong to CSS, behaviour belongs to JavaScript. Every Skillzify page starts as plain HTML text that the browser turns into a tree of elements called the DOM.

2. The essential tags

Most pages use a small set of tags. Headings run from h1 (the page title, used once) down to h6. Paragraphs use p. Links use a with an href attribute. Images use img with src and alt text that screen readers read aloud. Lists come in two kinds: ul for unordered bullets and ol for numbered steps, each holding li items.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><title>Skillzify Mini</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Learn Python</h1>
  <p>Start with <a href="/lessons">the lesson list</a>.</p>
  <img src="logo.png" alt="Skillzify logo">
  <ul><li>Variables</li><li>Loops</li><li>Functions</li></ul>
</body>
</html>

3. Nesting and attributes

Tags nest inside each other like boxes inside boxes, and every opening tag needs its closing tag. Attributes add information: href tells a link where to go, src tells an image what to load. A page that validates cleanly renders predictably in every browser, which is why Skillzify keeps its markup simple and consistent across all 17 pages.

4. Why this matters for Skillzify

Skillzify lessons, exercises and reference entries are all HTML at heart. When you can read raw HTML fluently, you can debug any page by viewing its source instead of guessing what went wrong.
lessons.task: Build a one-page profile for yourself: one h1, two h2 sections, three paragraphs, a link to your GitHub, one image with alt text, and a 5-item unordered list of skills. Open it in the browser and check it with the W3C validator.
checks: Why should a page have exactly one h1?
The h1 is the page title. Screen readers and search engines use it to understand the page topic; multiple h1s blur that meaning.
What is alt text on an image actually for?
It describes the image for screen readers and shows when the image fails to load. It is accessibility, not decoration.
interview: Explain the difference between a block element and an inline element.
Block elements like p and h1 start on a new line and take full width; inline elements like a and strong flow inside a line of text.
What does DOCTYPE do?
It tells the browser to render the page in standards mode instead of quirks mode, so layout rules behave consistently.

lessons.t: HTML Base 2 — Tables, Forms, Inputs, Semantic Layout
lessons.sub: Data on a page and data from the user
lessons.goal: By the end you can build a table, a working form with the right input types, and a page laid out with semantic tags instead of divs everywhere.
lessons.body:
1. Tables for tabular data

Tables are for data with rows and columns, never for layout. A table uses table, thead for the header row, tbody for the body, tr for each row, and th for header cells and td for data cells. Skillzify uses tables in reference pages where comparing values side by side is the whole point.

2. Forms collect user input

A form wraps inputs and a submit button. Each input needs a label linked by for and id, so clicking the label focuses the field and screen readers announce it. The right input type matters: email brings up the right mobile keyboard and validates format, number restricts to digits, password hides the text, and select and textarea cover choices and long text.

<form action="/api/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
  <label for="level">Level</label>
  <select id="level" name="level">
    <option>Beginner</option><option>Intermediate</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

3. Semantic layout

Replace generic divs with tags that mean something: header for the top, nav for links, main for the one main content area, section for themed chunks, article for self-contained pieces, and footer for the close. Skillzify pages use exactly this skeleton, which is why its shared nav can be injected into one placeholder on every page.

4. Built-in validation

Attributes like required, minlength, min and max give you free validation before JavaScript ever runs. The browser blocks submission and shows a message. Never rely on it alone, though: real validation always happens again on the server.
lessons.task: Build a Skillzify signup form: name (text, required), email (email, required), password (minlength 8), level (select), and a checkbox for terms. Submit it empty and watch the browser block it; then fill it in and confirm it passes.
checks: Why link a label to its input with for and id?
Clicking the label focuses the field, and screen readers announce the label when the field is focused — without it, the field is unnamed to assistive tech.
Why is browser form validation not enough on its own?
Anyone can bypass the browser with curl or DevTools, so the server must validate every field again. Browser validation is only a convenience.
interview: When should you use a table, and when should you not?
Use tables for genuinely tabular data like scores or schedules. Never use them for page layout — that job belongs to Flexbox and Grid.
What is the difference between GET and POST on a form?
GET puts data in the URL and is for safe reads; POST puts data in the body and is for actions that change something, like signup or login.

lessons.t: CSS Base — Selectors, Colours, Fonts, Box Model
lessons.sub: Making the skeleton look like a product
lessons.goal: By the end you can style a page with selectors, colours, fonts and spacing, and explain the box model well enough to predict why an element is the size it is.
lessons.body:
1. Selectors target elements

CSS rules are selector plus declarations. An element selector like p styles every paragraph; a class like .card styles anything with that class; an id like #nav styles one element. Classes are the workhorse: reusable, combinable, and the reason Skillzify can style 250 lesson cards with a handful of rules.

2. Colours and fonts

Colours are written as hex values like #6c7bff, rgb, or named colours. Fonts are set with font-family, usually a stack that falls back gracefully, and sized with font-size and font-weight. Skillzify loads Manrope for text and JetBrains Mono for code from Google Fonts, then falls back to system fonts if the network is slow.

.card {
  background: #111c33;
  color: #f2f4f7;
  font-family: Manrope, system-ui, sans-serif;
  padding: 18px;
  border: 1px solid #1e2d4d;
  border-radius: 18px;
  margin-bottom: 14px;
}

3. The box model

Every element is a box: content in the middle, then padding inside, then border, then margin outside. The trap is that by default width covers only the content, so padding and border inflate the real size. Skillzify opens its stylesheet with box-sizing: border-box on everything, making width mean the whole box. That single line prevents half of all beginner layout bugs.

4. Specificity and the cascade

When two rules conflict, the more specific selector wins: id beats class, class beats element. Equal specificity goes to the later rule. Keep selectors short and flat, and you will rarely need to fight the cascade or reach for the !important escape hatch. When in doubt, inspect the element in DevTools: the computed styles panel shows exactly which rule won and which ones were overridden.
lessons.task: Style your B.1 profile page: a dark background, a card class with padding, border and rounded corners, a styled h1, and links in a single accent colour. Then add box-sizing border-box and measure a card's width in DevTools before and after.
checks: A box is width 200px with 20px padding on each side. How wide is it under content-box, and under border-box?
Content-box: 240px, because padding adds outside the width. Border-box: 200px, because padding is included inside the declared width.
Why prefer classes over ids for styling?
Classes are reusable and combinable, so one rule can style many elements; an id styles exactly one element and has very high specificity.
interview: Explain the CSS box model in one minute.
Content, padding, border, margin from inside out. Width defaults to content only, so border-box is the sane default that makes width mean the whole box.
How does the cascade decide which rule wins?
By specificity first — id beats class beats element — then by source order when specificity is equal.

lessons.t: CSS Base 2 — Flexbox, Grid, Positioning, Responsive Basics
lessons.sub: Layout that adapts to any screen
lessons.goal: By the end you can lay out a page with Flexbox and Grid, position elements deliberately, and make a layout collapse cleanly on a phone with media queries.
lessons.body:
1. Flexbox: layout along one axis

Flexbox arranges items in a row or a column. Set display: flex on the parent, then control spacing with justify-content along the main axis, align-items across it, and gap for even spacing. It is the right tool for nav bars, rows of cards, and centring one element inside another — the three layouts beginners fight with most.

2. Grid: layout in two dimensions

Grid handles rows and columns together. grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) makes three equal columns; gap spaces them. Skillzify uses Grid for its lesson cards and Flexbox inside each card. Rule of thumb: one axis, Flexbox; two axes, Grid.

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 14px;
}
@media (max-width: 820px) {
  .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}
.nav { position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 30; }

3. Positioning

Static is the default flow. Relative nudges an element from its normal spot. Absolute positions it against the nearest positioned ancestor, which is how badges and copy buttons sit inside code blocks. Fixed pins it to the viewport. Sticky, used for Skillzify's top bar, scrolls normally until it hits the top, then stays put.

4. Responsive basics

Media queries change the layout at a width breakpoint: three columns become one below 820px. Combine that with fluid widths like width: min(1140px, 92%) and images that never exceed their container, and one page works from a phone to a monitor without a separate mobile site. A handy habit is to design the mobile layout in a narrow browser window first, then widen it and add breakpoints only when the design starts to strain.
lessons.task: Rebuild your profile page layout: a sticky nav with Flexbox, a 3-column Grid of skill cards, and a media query that collapses the grid to one column under 700px. Resize the browser window and confirm the collapse happens.
checks: When do you reach for Grid instead of Flexbox?
When the layout needs rows and columns at once, like a card grid. Flexbox is for a single row or column.
What does position: sticky do that fixed does not?
Sticky scrolls with the page until it reaches its threshold, then sticks; fixed is pinned to the viewport from the start and never scrolls.
interview: Explain the difference between justify-content and align-items.
Justify-content aligns along the main axis (row direction by default); align-items aligns across the cross axis. Swap them mentally when flex-direction changes.
How would you make a page responsive without a framework?
Fluid widths, flexible images, Grid/Flexbox layouts, and media queries that reflow the layout at breakpoints — mobile-first if possible.

lessons.t: JavaScript Base — Variables, Data Types, Operators, Console
lessons.sub: Your first real programming language
lessons.goal: By the end you can declare variables correctly, use the core data types, combine values with operators, and debug with the console.
lessons.body:
1. Variables: const first, let when it changes

JavaScript has three ways to declare a variable, but only two should be used. const is for values that never get reassigned, let is for values that do, and var is legacy with confusing scoping rules. Skillzify code uses const by default, which makes it obvious at a glance what can change and what cannot.

2. Data types

The primitives are number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol and bigint. Strings hold text, numbers hold all numeric values (there is no separate integer type), booleans are true or false, and null means deliberately empty while undefined means never assigned. Objects and arrays hold structured data and are covered in the next lesson.

const xp = 120;
let streak = 5;
const name = "Vikas";
const isSignedIn = true;
console.log(name + " has " + xp + " XP");
console.log(typeof xp);        // "number"
console.log(10 % 3);           // 1, the remainder
streak += 1;
console.log(streak);           // 6

3. Operators

Arithmetic covers plus, minus, multiply, divide and remainder. Comparison operators like === and > return booleans. Always use strict equality ===: loose == coerces types and produces surprises like "5" == 5 being true. Logical operators &&, || and ! combine conditions.

4. The console is your lab

console.log prints values, console.table prints arrays and objects neatly, and the browser DevTools console lets you run any JavaScript against the live page. Skillzify exposes helpers like Skillzify.toast on the window object precisely so you can call them from the console while learning.
lessons.task: In the DevTools console, declare a const for your name, a let for XP, and add 20 XP with +=. Print a sentence combining them, check typeof on each variable, and deliberately compare "5" == 5 and "5" === 5 to see the difference.
checks: When do you use const, and when let?
const by default, for anything never reassigned; let only when the value genuinely changes, like a counter or a running total.
Why is === safer than ==?
=== compares value and type with no coercion; == converts types first, so "5" == 5 is true and hides bugs.
interview: What is the difference between null and undefined?
null is an intentional empty value assigned by the programmer; undefined means a variable was declared but never given a value, or a property does not exist.
What does typeof null return, and why is it famous?
It returns "object" — a historic bug in the language that was never fixed because too much code depends on it.

lessons.t: JavaScript Base 2 — Conditions, Loops, Functions, Arrays, Objects
lessons.sub: The building blocks of every program
lessons.goal: By the end you can write if/else logic, loops, reusable functions, and work with arrays and objects — the four constructs behind nearly all of Skillzify's client code.
lessons.body:
1. Conditions choose a path

if / else if / else runs different code based on a boolean test. A ternary, condition ? a : b, is the compact form for simple either-or values. Skillzify uses conditions everywhere: whether a lesson is unlocked, whether a streak continues, whether the user is signed in.

2. Loops repeat work

A for loop runs a fixed number of times, a while loop runs until a condition fails, and for...of walks through an array's values directly. Prefer for...of or array methods over manual index loops when you do not need the index — the code reads like a sentence instead of bookkeeping.

const lessons = [
  { id: "b-1", title: "Intro", xp: 20 },
  { id: "b-2", title: "Loops", xp: 20 }
];
function totalXp(list) {
  let total = 0;
  for (const lesson of list) { total += lesson.xp; }
  return total;
}
const user = { name: "Vikas", level: 3 };
console.log(user.name, totalXp(lessons));

3. Functions package behaviour

A function takes inputs, does work, and returns a result. Named functions, function expressions and arrow functions all exist; arrow functions are the compact form used in callbacks. The golden rule is one job per function, so each one is testable and its name explains it.

4. Arrays and objects

Arrays are ordered lists with methods like push, map and filter. Objects are key-value records accessed with dot notation. Skillzify's entire curriculum is arrays of lesson objects exactly like the example above, and progress is an object keyed by lesson id.
lessons.task: Write a small script: an array of 5 lesson objects with xp values, a function totalXp that sums them with a loop, and a function levelFor that returns Beginner under 100 XP, Intermediate under 300, else Advanced. Run it and test all three levels.
checks: Why prefer for...of over a C-style index loop when you only need values?
It removes index bookkeeping, so there is no off-by-one error possible and the intent — visit each item — is obvious.
What is the difference between an array and an object?
An array is an ordered list accessed by index; an object is a record accessed by named keys.
interview: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
undefined. The function still runs, but calling code receives undefined.
Explain the difference between a function declaration and an arrow function, briefly.
Declarations are hoisted and have their own this; arrow functions are compact, not hoisted the same way, and inherit this from the surrounding scope.

lessons.t: Python Base — Setup, Print/Input, Variables, Data Types
lessons.sub: Python from zero, the way Skillzify uses it
lessons.goal: By the end you can install Python, run a script in VS Code, read input from the user, and use variables and the core data types correctly.
lessons.body:
1. Setup: Python and VS Code

Install Python from python.org and tick the box that adds it to PATH, then install VS Code and the Python extension. Verify with python --version in the terminal. Skillzify's flowchart generators are Python scripts run exactly this way, so this setup is not a detour — it is the real toolchain.

2. Print and input

print writes to the screen and input reads a line of text from the user. Input always returns a string, so convert it with int or float before doing maths. This string-or-number confusion is the single most common beginner bug in Python.

name = input("Your name: ")
age = int(input("Your age: "))
score = 85.5
passed = score >= 50
print(name, "is", age, "and passed:", passed)
print(type(score))   # <class 'float'>
print(10 // 3)      # 3, floor division
print(2 ** 3)       # 8, exponent

3. Variables and types

Python variables need no declaration and no type annotation: assignment creates them. The core types are int, float, str, bool, plus the collections covered next lesson. Variables are names bound to values, and rebinding a name to a new value is normal and cheap.

4. Dynamic typing, with discipline

Because types are checked at runtime, a variable can hold a string in one line and a number in the next. That freedom is convenient and dangerous: name variables clearly, and convert input explicitly at the boundary, so type errors surface where the data enters, not deep inside the program. Run your script often as you write it: a small program tested line by line is far easier to fix than a long one run for the first time at the end.
lessons.task: Write a script that asks for a name and two numbers, prints their sum, difference and product, and prints the type of each result. Run it in VS Code, then run it again entering text instead of a number and read the error carefully.
checks: Why does input() need int() around it before maths?
input() always returns a string. Adding two strings concatenates them, and comparing a string to a number raises a TypeError.
What does 10 // 3 return, and how is it different from 10 / 3?
10 // 3 is 3, floor division that drops the remainder; 10 / 3 is 3.333..., true division.
interview: Is Python statically or dynamically typed?
Dynamically typed: variable types are decided at runtime and a name can be rebound to a value of a different type.
What happens if you add a string and a number in Python?
A TypeError at runtime. Python refuses implicit conversion between str and int, unlike JavaScript.

lessons.t: Python Base 2 — Conditions, Loops, Functions, Lists & Dicts
lessons.sub: Python that does real work
lessons.goal: By the end you can write Python with conditions, loops and functions, and choose between lists and dicts for the data in front of you.
lessons.body:
1. Conditions and loops

Python conditions use if / elif / else with indentation instead of braces. Loops use for over any sequence and while while a condition holds. Indentation is not style in Python — it is syntax, and inconsistent indentation is a hard error, not a warning.

2. Functions

Define functions with def, pass parameters, and return values. Default arguments make a parameter optional. Python functions can return multiple values as a tuple, which is how small helper functions in Skillzify's flowchart code return both a result and a status.

def grade(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 50:
        return "Pass"
    return "Fail"

lessons = [{"id": "p-1", "xp": 20}, {"id": "p-2", "xp": 30}]
progress = {"p-1": True, "p-2": False}
total = sum(l["xp"] for l in lessons if progress[l["id"]])
print(grade(85), total)   # Pass 20

3. Lists

Lists are ordered, mutable sequences. Index them, slice them, append to them, and loop over them directly instead of by index. List comprehensions build a new list from an old one in a single readable expression — the idiomatic Python way to map and filter.

4. Dicts

Dicts map keys to values and are Python's default data structure: progress["p-1"] looks up a lesson in constant time. Skillzify's flowchart parser produces nested dicts as its intermediate JSON, and the web side reads that JSON directly — one data shape, two languages. Dicts also power JSON itself, so every dict you write is practice for the real pipeline that carries flowchart data from Python to the browser.
lessons.task: Write a script with a list of 5 lesson dicts (id, title, xp) and a progress dict of completed ids. Compute total earned XP with a comprehension, then add a function grade that maps a percentage to A/Pass/Fail and print both results.
checks: Why iterate a list directly instead of by index in Python?
Direct iteration is shorter, cannot go out of bounds, and reads as intent. Indexes are only needed when the position itself matters.
When do you pick a dict over a list?
When you look things up by a key, like a lesson id. A dict lookup is O(1); scanning a list for an id is O(n).
interview: What is a list comprehension, and when is it the right choice?
A one-line expression building a list from another iterable, optionally filtered. Right for simple map/filter jobs; wrong when the logic needs several statements.
How does Python indentation relate to correctness?
Indentation defines block structure — it is syntax, not formatting. Wrong indentation changes meaning or raises an IndentationError.

lessons.t: Git Base — Init, Add, Commit, Push, GitHub Basics
lessons.sub: Version control from your first commit
lessons.goal: By the end you can initialise a repo, stage and commit changes, push to GitHub, and explain what each step actually does.
lessons.body:
1. Git tracks snapshots, not files

Git records snapshots of your project over time. Each commit is a checkpoint with a message, a timestamp and a parent commit, forming a history you can rewind. Skillzify's entire history lives this way: every feature, fix and refactor is a commit you can inspect, which is why a bug can be traced to the exact change that introduced it.

2. The core workflow

Four commands cover daily work. git init creates a repo. git add stages changes into the next snapshot. git commit -m records the snapshot with a message. git push sends commits to GitHub, the remote copy. git status and git log show where you stand and what happened before.

git init
 git add .
 git commit -m "Add lesson list page"
 git branch -M main
 git remote add origin https://github.com/vikaspatil06/demo.git
 git push -u origin main
# later, each change is:
 git add . && git commit -m "Fix theme toggle" && git push

3. Commit messages are documentation

Write messages in the imperative mood describing what the change does: Add, Fix, Update, Remove. A future you, or a teammate, reads the log to understand why a line exists. Vague messages like update stuff are a small debt that compounds into an unreadable history.

4. Never commit secrets

API keys, passwords and service-account files must never reach GitHub. A .gitignore file lists paths Git skips, and a committed .env.example shows the shape of the config without the values. Skillzify's Firebase web config is public by design, but its Gemini key lives only in environment variables on Render.
lessons.task: Create a practice repo: init it, add a .gitignore with node_modules and .env, commit a small HTML file, create the repo on GitHub, and push. Then make a second commit fixing one line and push again; check git log shows both.
checks: What is the difference between git add and git commit?
add stages changes into the next snapshot; commit records that staged snapshot into history. Nothing is saved until you commit.
Why does a .env file belong in .gitignore?
It holds secrets like API keys. Once pushed to GitHub, a secret is public forever — even deleting it later leaves it in history.
interview: Explain the difference between git and GitHub.
Git is the version-control tool that runs locally and tracks history; GitHub is a hosting service for Git repos that adds collaboration, pull requests and CI.
What does git status tell you?
Which files are staged, modified, untracked or clean, and which branch you are on — the state of your working tree versus the last commit.

lessons.t: VS Code & Tools Base — Editor, Terminal, Extensions, Running Code Locally
lessons.sub: Your workshop, set up once and used daily
lessons.goal: By the end you can navigate VS Code fluently, use its integrated terminal, install the extensions that matter, and run a local server for any web project.
lessons.body:
1. The editor is the workshop

VS Code is where nearly all of this course happens. Learn its core moves: Ctrl+P to open any file by name, Ctrl+Shift+F to search the whole project, Ctrl+grave to toggle the terminal, and multi-cursor editing with Alt+Click. These four shortcuts alone save hours a week once they are muscle memory.

2. The integrated terminal

The terminal inside VS Code runs the same commands as a standalone one: node server.js starts a backend, python3 -m http.server 8080 serves a static site, git status checks your repo. Running the server from inside the editor keeps the code, the logs and the errors in one window.

# Serve any static site locally (Skillzify included)
python3 -m http.server 8080
# then open http://localhost:8080 in the browser
# Run a Node backend
node server.js
# Check what is listening on a port
# Windows: netstat -ano | findstr 8080

3. Extensions that earn their place

Install only extensions you will actually use: Python and Pylance for Python, ESLint and Prettier for JavaScript, Live Server for quick static previews, and GitLens for seeing who changed a line and when. Every extension costs startup time, so audit the list monthly and remove the ones you never open.

4. Running code locally, the habit

Every project in this course runs locally first: a static site on port 8080, a Node server on 3000, a Python script in the terminal. If it does not run on your machine, it does not ship — that discipline is what makes deployments boring instead of scary.
lessons.task: Set up a workspace folder for the course: open it in VS Code, install the Python and Live Server extensions, and serve a test HTML file on port 8080. Then use Ctrl+P to jump between two files and Ctrl+Shift+F to find a word across the folder.
checks: Why serve a static site over HTTP instead of opening the file directly?
File URLs block fetch, modules and some APIs for security; a local server behaves like production and avoids those restrictions.
What is the fastest way to open a file you know the name of?
Ctrl+P quick-open, then type a few letters of the filename — far faster than clicking through the folder tree.
interview: What is the difference between the VS Code terminal and a separate terminal app?
Nothing fundamental — it is the same shell embedded in the editor. The advantage is context: it opens in the project folder with the editor beside it.
Why keep your extension list small?
Each extension adds startup time, memory and potential conflicts. A lean list keeps the editor fast and the tooling predictable.

lessons.t: HTTP & DNS Deep — Requests, Responses, Status Codes
lessons.sub: What actually travels across the wire
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain DNS resolution, read an HTTP request and response, use status codes correctly, and debug a failed Skillzify API call in the Network tab.
lessons.body:
1. DNS: names to numbers

Computers talk to IP addresses, humans use names. DNS is the lookup system that turns skillzify-v2-staging.onrender.com into an IP. The browser checks its cache, then the OS cache, then asks a resolver, which walks from the root servers down to the authoritative server for the domain. A slow first visit is often DNS, not your code — and caching at each level is why repeat visits are fast.

2. HTTP requests and responses

Every web interaction is a request with a method, a path, headers and an optional body, answered by a response with a status code, headers and a body. GET reads, POST creates, PUT and PATCH update, DELETE removes. Headers carry metadata: Content-Type says the body is JSON, Authorization carries a token, Cache-Control says how long to keep a copy.

POST /api/tutor HTTP/1.1
Host: skillzify-v2-staging.onrender.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"question": "What is a closure?"}

-- response --
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"reply": "A closure is..."}

3. Status codes are a language

2xx means success, 3xx means redirect, 4xx means the client made a mistake (400 bad input, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), and 5xx means the server failed. Skillzify's API returns 429 when the rate limit fires and 400 when the question is empty — the frontend reads the code and shows the right message instead of guessing.

4. Debugging in the Network tab

Open DevTools, click Network, reload, and every request appears with its status, size and timing. Click one to see its headers and body. When a feature breaks, this tab tells you in seconds whether the problem is the request, the response, or the code that renders it.
lessons.task: With Skillzify running locally, open the Network tab, trigger the AI tutor, and inspect the request: method, URL, request body, status code and response body. Then change the question to an empty string and record the status code the server returns.
checks: What is the difference between a 401 and a 403?
401 means unauthenticated — no valid credentials were presented. 403 means authenticated but forbidden — the identity is known and still not allowed.
Why does fetch not reject on a 500 response?
fetch only rejects on network-level failures. An HTTP error status still resolves, so code must check res.ok or res.status itself.
interview: Walk me through DNS resolution for a URL you type.
Browser cache, then OS cache, then the resolver queries root, TLD and authoritative servers, returning the IP; the result is cached at each level.
What does a 429 status code mean, and how should a client handle it?
Too many requests — the client hit a rate limit. It should back off, wait, and retry later, ideally respecting a Retry-After header.

lessons.t: Browser Rendering & the Critical Rendering Path
lessons.sub: From HTML text to painted pixels
lessons.goal: By the end you can trace the critical rendering path — DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint — and explain what makes a page render slowly.
lessons.body:
1. The critical rendering path

Rendering has five stages. The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree and CSS into the CSSOM tree. It combines them into a render tree containing only visible elements with their computed styles. Then layout computes the exact position and size of every box, and paint fills in pixels. JavaScript can force extra rounds of this work, which is why where scripts sit matters.

2. What blocks rendering

CSS in the head blocks rendering until it is parsed, because painting without styles would flash unstyled content. Classic scripts block parsing while they download and run. That is the whole reason Skillzify loads its stylesheet in the head and its scripts at the end of the body: styles first so the first paint is correct, scripts last so content appears fast.

<!-- Render-blocking: CSS in head, scripts deferred -->
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css?v=29">
</head>
<body>
  <!-- page content paints before these run -->
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</body>

3. Layout thrashing and repaints

Reading a layout value like offsetHeight right after changing a style forces the browser to recalculate layout immediately — do that in a loop and the page stutters. Batch your reads, batch your writes, and prefer transform and opacity for animations because they skip layout and paint entirely, running on the compositor instead.

4. Measuring, not guessing

DevTools Performance records a page load frame by frame, and Lighthouse scores the experience. The metrics that matter are first paint, largest contentful paint, and interaction delay. Optimise the critical path — fewer blocking resources, smaller CSS, deferred scripts — and all three improve together.
lessons.task: Open Skillzify locally, record a Performance trace of a reload, and find the largest contentful paint time. Then move one script tag into the head, reload, and compare: note how the paint timing changes, then move it back.
checks: Why does CSS block rendering but images do not?
The browser needs the full CSSOM before it can compute styles for the render tree; images are just boxes with a size until they arrive, so painting can start without them.
Why are transform and opacity the cheapest properties to animate?
They run on the compositor thread and skip layout and paint — the browser just moves an already-painted layer.
interview: Explain the critical rendering path in order.
Parse HTML into the DOM, parse CSS into the CSSOM, combine into the render tree, run layout to compute geometry, then paint pixels — with JS able to trigger extra rounds.
What is layout thrashing?
Alternating style writes and layout reads in a loop, forcing the browser to recalculate layout on every iteration instead of once.

lessons.t: Responsive Design — One Page, Every Screen
lessons.sub: From a phone to a monitor without a second site
lessons.goal: By the end you can design mobile-first, choose breakpoints deliberately, and make a Skillzify-style page reflow cleanly from 360px to a wide monitor.
lessons.body:
1. Mobile-first thinking

Design for the smallest screen first, then add layout as space grows. The base styles are the phone layout; media queries with min-width add columns and spacing for larger screens. This keeps the mobile experience — where most learners actually arrive — deliberate instead of a squashed afterthought, and it keeps the CSS smaller because the common case needs no overrides.

2. Fluid foundations

Fixed pixel widths break on small screens. Use percentages and flexible units for containers, min() to cap a width, and clamp() for type that scales smoothly between a floor and a ceiling. Skillzify's container is width: min(1140px, 92%): full width on a phone, capped on a monitor, with no media query needed at all.

.container { width: min(1140px, 92%); margin: 0 auto; }
h1 { font-size: clamp(28px, 5vw, 44px); }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
@media (min-width: 820px) {
  .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
}

3. Breakpoints are content decisions

Do not copy breakpoints from a framework blindly. Add a breakpoint where your content actually breaks: where a line gets too long, a card gets too narrow, or a nav wraps badly. Skillzify collapses its three-column grids to one column below 820px because that is where the cards stop being readable, not because a guide said so.

4. Touch and testing

On touch screens, targets need to be at least 44px tall, hover-only interactions must have a tap equivalent, and text must stay legible without zooming. Test by resizing the browser, then on a real phone: DevTools device mode simulates size, but only a real device shows true touch behaviour and font rendering.
lessons.task: Take your profile page and make it mobile-first: single column by default, two columns above 700px, three above 1100px. Set the h1 with clamp, make images max-width 100 percent, and test at 360px, 768px and 1280px widths in DevTools.
checks: What does width: min(1140px, 92%) do on a 400px phone and on a 2000px monitor?
On the phone it is 92 percent of 400px; on the monitor it caps at 1140px instead of stretching the full width.
Why design mobile-first instead of desktop-first?
The phone layout is the constrained, most-used case; adding layout as space grows is simpler than removing it, and the base CSS stays lean.
interview: How do you choose a breakpoint?
Where the content breaks — text too narrow, cards too cramped, nav wrapping — not from a fixed list of device sizes.
What is the viewport meta tag, and what breaks without it?
It sets layout width equal to device width. Without it, phones assume a 980px layout and shrink the page, breaking all responsive rules.

lessons.t: Forms & Validation — Trust Nothing the Browser Sends
lessons.sub: Client convenience, server authority
lessons.goal: By the end you can build an accessible form with layered validation, explain why client checks are only a courtesy, and write the server-side validation Skillzify relies on.
lessons.body:
1. Forms are a contract

A form promises the user what will happen and promises the server what shape the data arrives in. Every field needs a label, a name, the right type, and a clear error state. Skillzify's signup and login forms follow this exactly: email type for email, password type for passwords, and required on the fields that must be present.

2. Client-side validation is UX, not security

HTML attributes like required, minlength and pattern, plus JavaScript checks on submit, give instant feedback without a round trip. They catch honest mistakes early. But they run in the user's browser, which the user controls — anyone can disable them, edit the page, or send a request with curl. Treat client validation as a courtesy for real users.

// Server-side: the only validation that counts
app.post("/api/signup", (req, res) => {
  const email = String(req.body.email || "").trim();
  if (!email.includes("@") || email.length > 200) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: "Valid email required" });
  }
  res.json({ ok: true });
});

3. Server-side validation is the gate

The server re-checks everything: presence, type, length, format and range. It rejects with a 400 and a specific message, never a stack trace. It also enforces size limits on the body itself, so a megabyte of junk in one field cannot exhaust memory. Skillzify's AI routes do exactly this before any Gemini call is made.

4. Accessible errors

Errors must be visible, specific and announced. Put the message next to the field, link it with aria-describedby, move focus to the first invalid field, and never rely on colour alone. A form that fails silently for a keyboard or screen-reader user is a broken form, however pretty it looks.
lessons.task: Build a feedback form with name, email and message fields. Add HTML validation, then a JavaScript check that shows inline errors. Finally write a tiny Express route that re-validates the same three fields server-side and returns 400 with a message for each failure.
checks: Why must the server validate a field the browser already validated?
Browser validation can be bypassed entirely with curl or DevTools. The server is the only code you control, so it is the only trustworthy gate.
What should a server return when validation fails, and what must it never return?
A 400 with a specific, user-safe message per field. Never a stack trace or internal detail that leaks how the server works.
interview: Explain defence in depth for a form.
Layered checks: HTML attributes for instant UX, JavaScript for richer feedback, server validation as the authority, and size limits plus rate limits against abuse.
How do you make form errors accessible?
Message beside the field, linked with aria-describedby, focus moved to the first error, and meaning conveyed by text, not colour alone.

lessons.t: CSS Animations & Transitions — Motion with Purpose
lessons.sub: Small movements that teach, not distract
lessons.goal: By the end you can add transitions and keyframe animations, choose the cheap properties to animate, and respect users who prefer reduced motion.
lessons.body:
1. Transitions: between two states

A transition animates a property change over time: a button darkens on hover, a card lifts slightly, a theme toggle fades instead of snapping. You declare which property, how long, and what easing curve. Skillzify's buttons and cards use short 150–250ms transitions — long enough to feel smooth, short enough to never feel slow.

2. Keyframes: full choreography

When a change has more than two states, keyframes describe the whole sequence: a spinner rotating, a toast sliding in, a skeleton shimmer. The animation property names the keyframes, sets duration, iteration and fill mode. Reusable keyframe names in one stylesheet keep motion consistent across the site.

.btn { transition: background 0.2s ease, transform 0.2s ease; }
.btn:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
@keyframes slideIn {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px); }
  to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}
.toast { animation: slideIn 0.25s ease-out; }

3. Animate the cheap properties

Transform and opacity run on the compositor thread and skip layout and paint, so they stay at 60 frames per second even on weak phones. Animating width, height, top or margin forces layout recalculation every frame and stutters. If a motion idea needs a layout property, redesign the motion instead of accepting the jank.

4. Respect reduced motion

Some users experience motion sickness or distraction from animation. The prefers-reduced-motion media query lets you disable or shorten animations for them. It is one block of CSS, it costs nothing, and it is the difference between polish and a product that harms part of its audience.
lessons.task: Add to your profile page: a button hover lift with a 0.2s transition, a toast that slides in with keyframes, and a prefers-reduced-motion block that turns both animations off. Test by enabling reduced motion in your OS settings.
checks: Why animate transform instead of top or margin?
Transform runs on the compositor and skips layout and paint; top and margin force layout recalculation every frame, which stutters.
What does prefers-reduced-motion do, and why use it?
It detects the user's OS setting asking for less animation. Honouring it prevents motion sickness and distraction for users who need it.
interview: What is the difference between a transition and an animation?
A transition animates between two states when a property changes; an animation runs a defined keyframe sequence, possibly looping, without needing a state change.
How do you keep animations at 60fps?
Animate only transform and opacity, keep durations short, and avoid triggering layout or paint on each frame.

lessons.t: Accessibility — Building for Everyone
lessons.sub: a11y is a feature, not a favour
lessons.goal: By the end you can audit a page for the core accessibility failures, fix them with semantic HTML, ARIA and keyboard support, and explain why accessibility is also good engineering.
lessons.body:
1. Who accessibility is for

Accessibility means the page works for people using screen readers, keyboards, voice control, magnification, or high-contrast settings — and for everyone on a cracked phone screen in bright sunlight. Around one in six people live with a disability, and interviewers increasingly ask about this because products that exclude users lose users.

2. Semantic HTML does most of the work

Real buttons, real links, real headings in order, labelled form fields and alt text on images give assistive technology the structure it needs for free. A div with an onclick is invisible to a keyboard user; a button works with Enter, Space, focus rings and screen readers with zero extra code. Skillzify's nav and forms use real elements for exactly this reason.

<!-- Accessible: real button, labelled, focusable -->
<button aria-label="Toggle dark mode">🌙</button>
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" aria-describedby="email-hint">
<p id="email-hint">We never share your email.</p>

3. ARIA fills the gaps

ARIA attributes describe what HTML cannot: aria-label names an icon-only button, aria-describedby links a hint to its field, aria-live announces dynamic changes like a toast, and roles describe custom widgets. Rule one of ARIA: do not use it when a native element already does the job. Rule two: a wrong ARIA attribute is worse than none.

4. Contrast, focus and testing

Text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, and focus must always be visible — never remove the outline without replacing it. Test by tabbing through the whole page with the keyboard alone, then run a screen reader for five minutes. Automated checkers catch roughly a third of issues; the keyboard test catches the rest.
lessons.task: Audit your profile page: tab through it using only the keyboard, check every image has alt text, every input has a label, and headings are in order. Fix what fails, then run the Lighthouse accessibility audit and record the score before and after.
checks: Why is a real button better than a clickable div?
A button is focusable, works with Enter and Space, announces itself to screen readers, and shows a focus ring — a div does none of that without manual work.
When should you use ARIA, and when should you avoid it?
Use ARIA only when no native HTML element expresses the meaning; prefer native elements first, because a wrong ARIA attribute is worse than none.
interview: What is the first rule of ARIA?
Do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already provides the semantics — native elements are tested, free and reliable.
How do you test accessibility beyond automated tools?
Keyboard-only navigation through the whole page, a screen reader pass, and manual checks of contrast, focus visibility and heading order.

lessons.t: Closures & Scope — Functions That Remember
lessons.sub: Where variables live and how long they last
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain lexical scope, write a closure, and use closures for private state — the pattern behind Skillzify's storage helpers and counters.
lessons.body:
1. Scope is where a name is visible

JavaScript has global scope, function scope and block scope. A variable declared inside a block with let or const exists only in that block; a variable declared inside a function exists only in that function. Inner code can read outer variables, but outer code cannot read inner ones. This one-way visibility is lexical scope, decided by where the code is written, not where it runs.

2. A closure is a function plus its birthplace

When a function is created inside another function, it keeps a live reference to the outer function's variables even after the outer function has returned. That remembered environment is a closure. It is not a special feature you opt into — every function in JavaScript is a closure over the scope where it was defined.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;              // private: only the closure sees it
  return function () {
    count += 1;
    return count;
  };
}
const xpCounter = makeCounter();
xpCounter(); // 1
xpCounter(); // 2 — count survived between calls

3. Private state without classes

Closures create genuinely private variables: nothing outside can touch count except through the returned function. Skillzify uses this shape in app.js, where an IIFE wraps private helpers and exposes only a small public API on window.Skillzify. The same pattern powers counters, caches and rate limiters across the codebase.

4. The classic closure trap

Looping with var and creating callbacks inside the loop used to capture one shared variable, so every callback saw the final value. let fixes it because each iteration gets its own binding. When a bug smells like every handler doing the same thing, check whether a closure is sharing a variable you thought was per-item.
lessons.task: Write makeCounter as above, plus a makeBank that returns deposit and getBalance functions sharing one private balance. Prove the balance is private by trying to read it directly from outside and confirming it is undefined.
checks: What is a closure, in one sentence?
A function that retains access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished executing.
Why does let fix the classic loop-closure bug but var does not?
let creates a fresh binding per loop iteration, so each callback captures its own value; var has one function-scoped binding shared by all callbacks.
interview: How would you create private state in JavaScript without a class?
A closure: an outer function holds the variable and returns inner functions that read and update it; nothing outside can reach the variable directly.
Explain lexical scope vs dynamic scope.
Lexical scope resolves names by where code is written; dynamic scope would resolve by where it runs. JavaScript is lexical.

lessons.t: this & Prototypes — How JavaScript Objects Really Work
lessons.sub: The prototype chain, demystified
lessons.goal: By the end you can predict what this refers to in any call, explain the prototype chain, and read class syntax as sugar over prototypes.
lessons.body:
1. this depends on the call, not the definition

In JavaScript, this is set by how a function is called. Called as a method, this is the object before the dot. Called plainly, this is undefined in strict mode. Called with new, this is the fresh object being built. Arrow functions are the exception: they inherit this from the surrounding scope and cannot be rebound. Most this bugs come from passing a method as a callback and losing its object.

2. Prototypes: shared behaviour

Every object has a hidden link to a prototype object. When you read a property the object lacks, JavaScript walks up the prototype chain until it finds it. Methods live on the prototype, not on each instance, so a thousand lesson objects share one set of methods instead of each carrying copies.

function Lesson(id, title) {
  this.id = id;
  this.title = title;
}
Lesson.prototype.summary = function () {
  return this.id + ": " + this.title;
};
const l = new Lesson("b-1", "Intro");
console.log(l.summary());   // "b-1: Intro"
console.log(l.hasOwnProperty("summary")); // false — it lives on the prototype

3. Classes are sugar

The class keyword writes the same prototype machinery with cleaner syntax: methods go on the prototype automatically, and extends sets up the chain. Skillzify's vanilla code mostly uses factory functions and plain objects instead, but interviewers and libraries assume you can read class syntax fluently.

4. When this goes wrong

Event handlers, timers and array callbacks all change the call site, so this changes too. The fixes are an arrow function that captures the outer this, bind to lock it, or avoiding this entirely by using closures and plain data — the approach Skillzify's modules mostly take.
lessons.task: Build a Lesson constructor with a prototype method summary and a prototype property xp defaulting to 20. Create two instances, override xp on one, and show the other still reads 20 — proving the prototype is shared, not copied.
checks: What decides the value of this inside a function?
How the function is called: as a method it is the object before the dot; plainly it is undefined in strict mode; with new it is the new object; arrows inherit it.
Where do methods live when you use a constructor function?
On the constructor's prototype object, shared by all instances. hasOwnProperty on an instance returns false for them.
interview: Explain the prototype chain in one minute.
Objects link to a prototype; a missing property is looked up the chain until found or the chain ends at null. Methods live on prototypes so instances share them.
Why does passing obj.method as a callback break this?
The call site changes, so this is no longer obj. Fix it with an arrow wrapper, bind, or by not relying on this.

lessons.t: Event Loop Deep — How JavaScript Never Blocks
lessons.sub: Call stack, queues, and the single thread
lessons.goal: By the end you can trace any async snippet through the call stack, microtask queue and task queue, and explain why a long loop freezes the page.
lessons.body:
1. One thread, three structures

JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack for what is executing now, a heap for objects, and queues for what is waiting. The event loop watches the stack: when it empties, it moves the next queued callback onto it. Nothing runs in parallel in your code; concurrency comes from the browser or Node doing slow work (network, timers, disk) off-thread and queueing the result.

2. Microtasks beat macrotasks

Promise callbacks go to the microtask queue; timers, events and I/O go to the task queue. After every stack emptying, the loop drains the entire microtask queue before touching one task. That is why a resolved promise's then always runs before a setTimeout with zero delay, and why a microtask that keeps queueing microtasks can starve everything else.

console.log("1");
setTimeout(function () { console.log("2"); }, 0);
Promise.resolve().then(function () { console.log("3"); });
console.log("4");
// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2 — promises jump the timer queue

3. Blocking is a choice

A synchronous loop that runs for two seconds freezes the page for two seconds: no clicks, no paints, no timers fire, because the stack never empties. The fix is to chunk heavy work with setTimeout or queueMicrotask, move it to a Web Worker, or make it async so the loop can breathe between pieces. Skillzify's rendering stays fast because it never does heavy synchronous work on the main thread.

4. Async/await is syntax, not magic

await pauses the function, not the thread: the function returns a pending promise, the loop keeps serving other work, and the function resumes from the microtask queue when the awaited promise settles. The event loop is the machinery underneath every async function you have written.
lessons.task: Predict the output order of the snippet above, then run it. Next, write a version with a promise that queues another promise inside its then, and a setTimeout of 0, and predict that order too before running it.
checks: Why does a resolved promise's then run before a zero-delay setTimeout?
Promise callbacks use the microtask queue, which the event loop drains fully before taking the next task from the timer queue.
Why does a long synchronous loop freeze the whole page?
The single thread is busy, so the call stack never empties and the event loop cannot run renders, timers or event handlers.
interview: Explain the event loop in one minute.
Single thread plus queues: the loop moves callbacks from the task and microtask queues onto the call stack when it empties; slow work happens off-thread and its completion is queued.
What is the difference between the microtask queue and the task queue?
Microtasks (promises) drain fully before each task; tasks (timers, events, I/O) run one per loop turn.

lessons.t: DOM Events & Delegation — Listening Smart
lessons.sub: Bubbling, capturing, and one listener for a thousand elements
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain event bubbling, use delegation to handle dynamic lists with a single listener, and stop memory leaks from orphaned listeners.
lessons.body:
1. Events travel in three phases

When a user clicks a button inside a card inside a page, the event travels down from the window to the target (capturing), fires at the target, then bubbles back up through every ancestor. addEventListener listens on the bubbling phase by default. Understanding this journey is the key to everything else in this lesson, because it means ancestors can hear events from descendants.

2. Delegation: one listener, endless children

Instead of attaching a listener to every lesson card, attach one to their shared parent and check event.target to see which child was actually clicked. New cards added later work automatically, because the parent was already listening. Skillzify's Learn page renders 250 lessons from data — delegation is the only sane way to wire them all.

document.getElementById("lessonList").addEventListener("click", function (e) {
  const card = e.target.closest(".lesson-card");
  if (!card) return;               // click was not on a card
  openLesson(card.dataset.id);     // one listener serves all cards
});

3. Controlling the flow

stopPropagation halts the journey so ancestors never hear the event; preventDefault stops the browser's default action, like following a link or submitting a form. Use both sparingly — stopping propagation can break other features listening higher up, and preventing defaults on the wrong element breaks accessibility.

4. Listeners and memory

Every listener holds a reference to its element. Remove an element without removing its listeners and the memory can linger. Delegation avoids this almost entirely: one listener on a long-lived parent, no per-item cleanup, and dynamic content that just works.
lessons.task: Build a list of 20 items rendered from an array with a single delegated click listener that logs the clicked item's id. Add 5 more items dynamically and confirm they work without adding any listeners. Then add a button inside one item that uses stopPropagation.
checks: Why does event delegation work for elements added after the listener was attached?
The listener lives on the parent, and events from new children still bubble up to it — the parent never needed to know the children existed.
What does e.target.closest do, and why is it useful here?
It walks up from the clicked element to the nearest ancestor matching the selector, so clicks on a card's inner text or icon still resolve to the card.
interview: Explain event bubbling and capturing.
Capturing travels from window down to the target; bubbling travels back up through ancestors. Listeners default to bubbling.
When would you use stopPropagation, and what is the risk?
To keep an event from reaching ancestors, e.g. a button inside a card. The risk is silently breaking other features that listen higher up.

lessons.t: Error Handling & Debugging — Finding Bugs Like a Professional
lessons.sub: Try/catch, stack traces, and DevTools as a lab
lessons.goal: By the end you can handle errors with try/catch and finally, read a stack trace to the exact failing line, and debug systematically with breakpoints instead of guessing.
lessons.body:
1. Errors are values with a story

JavaScript errors are objects with a name, a message and a stack trace showing the call chain that led to the failure. ReferenceError means a name does not exist, TypeError means a value was used the wrong way (like calling a non-function), and SyntaxError means the code could not even parse. Reading the error type first, before the message, already narrows the search.

2. try/catch/finally

Wrap code that can fail — JSON parsing, network calls, localStorage access — in try, handle the failure in catch, and put cleanup in finally, which runs either way. Skillzify wraps every localStorage read in try/catch because one corrupted value must never take down a page. Catch only what you can handle; rethrow the rest.

function loadProgress() {
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem("skillzify_progress");
    return raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : {};
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn("Corrupt progress, starting fresh:", err.message);
    return {};
  } finally {
    console.log("Progress load attempted");
  }
}

3. Debugging with breakpoints

console.log is the start, not the end. In DevTools Sources, click a line number to set a breakpoint, reload, and the code pauses there: inspect every variable, step line by line, and watch expressions change. Conditional breakpoints pause only when a value matches, which is how you catch a bug that happens once in a thousand iterations.

4. A debugging method

Reproduce it reliably, read the exact error, form one hypothesis, test it with the smallest change, and verify the fix removes the symptom without breaking anything else. Guess-and-check feels faster and is slower; a written hypothesis is what separates a professional debug session from an afternoon lost to random edits.
lessons.task: Take a small script with a deliberate bug (a JSON.parse on a bad string and a function called before it is defined). Reproduce the errors, read both stack traces, fix each with a minimal change, and add a try/catch that degrades gracefully.
checks: Why wrap localStorage reads in try/catch?
Stored data can be corrupted, the quota can be exceeded, or storage can be disabled — any of which throws, and one throw must not crash the page.
When should you rethrow an error instead of handling it?
When the local code cannot meaningfully recover — log context, then let the caller or a top-level handler decide.
interview: What is the difference between a SyntaxError and a TypeError?
SyntaxError means the code could not parse at all; TypeError means parsed code ran but used a value incorrectly, like calling something that is not a function.
Walk me through debugging a bug you cannot reproduce reliably.
Narrow the conditions, add logging at boundaries, use conditional breakpoints, and bisect recent changes until the trigger is isolated.

lessons.t: Data Structures Deep — Lists, Dicts, Sets, Tuples
lessons.sub: Choosing the right container changes everything
lessons.goal: By the end you can pick the right Python container for any job, reason about its time complexity, and explain why Skillzify's flowchart code uses dicts as its core shape.
lessons.body:
1. Lists: ordered and mutable

Lists hold an ordered sequence you can index, slice, append to and sort. Indexing and appending are fast, but inserting in the middle or checking membership with in scans the whole list. Use lists when order matters and you mostly append and iterate — like Skillzify's ordered lesson arrays.

2. Dicts: lookup by key

Dicts map keys to values with average O(1) lookup, insert and delete. They are Python's default structure for records, configs and indexes. Skillzify's flowchart parser builds nested dicts as its intermediate JSON, and the web side consumes the same shape — one data format understood by both languages.

seen = set()
progress = {"p-1": True, "p-2": False}
scores = [88, 92, 74, 91]
record = ("p-1", 88)          # tuple: a fixed, immutable pair
for lesson_id in progress:
    if lesson_id not in seen:
        seen.add(lesson_id)
print(len(seen), max(scores))  # 2 92

3. Sets: uniqueness and membership

Sets hold unique items with O(1) membership tests. Need to know whether a lesson was already counted, or deduplicate a list? A set is the answer. Checking in on a list inside a loop is the classic O(n squared) accident; a set makes the same check constant-time.

4. Tuples: fixed records

Tuples are immutable, ordered records — a coordinate, a lesson id plus a score, a key for a dict. Immutability makes them hashable, so they can be dict keys and set members where lists cannot. Choosing tuple over list signals intent: this record is complete and will not change.
lessons.task: Given a list of 1,000 lesson attempts with duplicate ids, use a set to count unique lessons, a dict to keep the best score per lesson, and a list to hold the final ranking sorted by score. Time the set-based dedup against a list-based one.
checks: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
A set is a hash table, so lookup is average O(1); a list must scan each element, O(n).
When would you choose a tuple over a list?
When the record is fixed and should never change — immutability documents intent and lets it be used as a dict key or set member.
interview: List vs tuple vs set vs dict — one line each.
List: ordered mutable sequence. Tuple: fixed immutable record. Set: unique items with fast membership. Dict: key-to-value lookup.
What is the complexity trap of using in on a list inside a loop?
Each check scans the list, so the loop becomes O(n squared). A set makes each check O(1).

lessons.t: OOP Inheritance & Polymorphism — Sharing Behaviour Safely
lessons.sub: Is-a relationships without the spaghetti
lessons.goal: By the end you can design a class hierarchy with inheritance, override methods polymorphically, and know when composition beats inheritance.
lessons.body:
1. Inheritance shares behaviour

A subclass inherits the methods and attributes of its parent, then adds or overrides what is specific. A QuizExercise and a CodeExercise can both inherit from Exercise, sharing scoring and timing while each implements its own render method. Inheritance models a genuine is-a relationship: a quiz exercise is an exercise.

2. Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours

Polymorphism means calling the same method on different objects and getting each object's own behaviour. A loop over exercises calling render works for every subclass without knowing which type it holds. Duck typing takes this further in Python: if it has the method, it can be used — no shared parent required.

class Exercise:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
    def render(self):
        return "Exercise: " + self.title

class QuizExercise(Exercise):
    def render(self):
        return "Quiz: " + self.title + " [4 options]"

for ex in [Exercise("Loops"), QuizExercise("Arrays")]:
    print(ex.render())

3. super and method resolution

super() calls the parent's version of a method, so a subclass can extend behaviour instead of replacing it. Python resolves methods along the method resolution order, which matters in multiple inheritance — keep hierarchies shallow so the order never becomes a puzzle.

4. Composition over inheritance

Deep inheritance trees become rigid: changing a parent ripples everywhere. Composition assembles behaviour from parts — an exercise has a scorer and a renderer — and stays flexible. Prefer inheritance for a true is-a relationship with shared behaviour, composition for everything else. A practical test is the sentence check: if you cannot say a QuizExercise is an Exercise in plain English, inheritance is the wrong tool and composition is the better design.
lessons.task: Model Skillzify exercises: a base Exercise class with title and score, a QuizExercise subclass that overrides render, and a CodeExercise subclass that adds a run method. Build a list of mixed exercises and render them all through one polymorphic loop.
checks: What is polymorphism, in the context of the code above?
Calling render on different exercise objects produces each class's own output through one shared interface — the caller never checks the type.
Why is composition often preferred over deep inheritance?
Inheritance couples subclasses tightly to parents, so changes ripple; composition assembles behaviour from parts that can be swapped independently.
interview: Inheritance vs composition — when each?
Inheritance for a genuine is-a relationship with shared behaviour; composition by default, because it stays flexible and avoids fragile base-class problems.
What does super() do in Python?
It calls the parent class's version of a method, letting a subclass extend behaviour instead of fully replacing it.

lessons.t: Comprehensions & Decorators — Pythonic Power Tools
lessons.sub: Shorter code that says more
lessons.goal: By the end you can write list, dict and set comprehensions fluently and build a decorator that wraps a function with extra behaviour.
lessons.body:
1. Comprehensions: collections in one line

A comprehension builds a collection from another iterable with an optional filter, reading like a sentence: squares of the numbers that are even. List, dict and set comprehensions all exist. They replace the two-line pattern of creating an empty collection and appending in a loop — the single most common Python idiom, and the one Skillzify's flowchart code uses to transform parsed nodes.

2. When not to use them

A comprehension with nested loops and two conditions stops being readable and becomes a puzzle. If the logic needs several statements, side effects, or error handling, a plain loop is the honest choice. Readability is the test, not brevity.

scores = [88, 92, 74, 91]
passed = [s for s in scores if s >= 50]
by_id = {"p-" + str(i): s for i, s in enumerate(scores)}

def timed(fn):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        import time
        start = time.time()
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        print(fn.__name__, "took", round(time.time() - start, 3), "s")
        return result
    return wrapper

3. Decorators wrap functions

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one with added behaviour — timing, logging, caching, access checks — without touching the original code. The @ syntax applies it at definition. The wrapper must accept *args and **kwargs and return the result, or it breaks the function it decorates.

4. Where you will meet them

Flask and FastAPI use decorators for routes, pytest uses them for fixtures, and functools.lru_cache memoises expensive calls with one line. Recognising the pattern means you can read framework code instead of fearing it.
lessons.task: Rewrite three loops as comprehensions: filter passing scores, build a dict of lesson id to XP, and collect unique tags into a set. Then write a @timed decorator and apply it to a function that sums a million numbers.
checks: When is a comprehension the wrong tool?
When the logic needs multiple statements, side effects, or error handling — then a plain loop is clearer and correct.
What must a decorator wrapper do to preserve the wrapped function's behaviour?
Accept *args and **kwargs, call the original, and return its result — otherwise arguments or return values are lost.
interview: Explain what a decorator is and give a real use case.
A function that wraps another function to add behaviour like timing, logging or caching, applied with @ — e.g. Flask routes or lru_cache.
List comprehension vs generator expression — the difference?
A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory now; a generator expression yields items lazily, one at a time, using almost no memory.

lessons.t: File Handling — Reading, Writing, and JSON Pipelines
lessons.sub: Programs that remember things
lessons.goal: By the end you can read and write files safely with context managers, work with paths, and build a JSON pipeline like the one behind Skillzify's flowchart feature.
lessons.body:
1. Open, use, close — automatically

The with statement opens a file and guarantees it closes, even if an exception fires mid-read. Forgetting to close a file leaks handles and can lose buffered writes. Always use with, always specify the mode — r for reading, w for overwriting, a for appending — and always state the encoding explicitly as utf-8.

2. Text, lines and structured data

Read a whole file with read(), iterate lines with a for loop (which streams instead of loading everything), or read lines into a list when the file is small. For structured data, JSON is the lingua franca: json.load reads a file into dicts and lists, json.dump writes them back. Skillzify's flowchart generator writes exactly this JSON, and the web renderer reads it.

import json
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("progress.json")
data = {"lessons_done": ["p-1", "p-2"], "xp": 40}
path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
loaded = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print(loaded["xp"])   # 40

3. Paths with pathlib

pathlib.Path replaces string juggling with slashes: Path("data") / "file.json" works on every OS, and methods like exists(), read_text() and write_text() make file code read like plain English. Old os.path code still works, but pathlib is the modern default.

4. Large files stream, small files load

A gigabyte log file must be processed line by line, never loaded whole. A small config file can be read in one go. Choosing wrong in either direction costs memory or speed — and in a server, a whole-file read on a big upload is a denial-of-service hole.
lessons.task: Write a script that saves a progress dict to progress.json, reads it back, adds a new completed lesson, and writes it again. Then read a 10,000-line generated file line by line and count lines containing the word error without loading the whole file.
checks: Why is with open(...) better than open() followed by close()?
with guarantees the file closes even if an exception is raised in between; a manual close is skipped when an error jumps out of the block.
Why specify encoding=utf-8 explicitly?
The default encoding varies by platform, so a file written on Windows can fail to read on Linux. Explicit utf-8 makes behaviour identical everywhere.
interview: How do you process a file too large to fit in memory?
Stream it line by line with a for loop over the file object, or use a generator, so only one line is in memory at a time.
Why is JSON the right format for the flowchart pipeline?
It is structured, human-readable, and natively understood by both Python and JavaScript, so the parser and renderer share one format.

lessons.t: Error Handling — Exceptions, EAFP, and Clean Failures
lessons.sub: Code that fails gracefully instead of crashing
lessons.goal: By the end you can handle exceptions precisely, choose between EAFP and look-before-you-leap, and write code that fails with a useful message.
lessons.body:
1. Exceptions are the error system

When Python cannot do something — a missing file, a bad conversion, a missing key — it raises an exception that unwinds the call stack until something catches it. Uncaught, it crashes the program with a traceback. The traceback is a gift: it names the error type, the message, and the exact line and call chain that failed.

2. try/except/else/finally

try holds the risky code, except catches specific errors, else runs only when nothing failed, and finally always runs for cleanup. Catch the narrowest exception you can name — a bare except hides real bugs, including typos and keyboard interrupts, and makes debugging miserable.

def load_scores(path):
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            data = json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return {"scores": []}
    except json.JSONDecodeError as err:
        raise ValueError("Bad JSON in " + path + ": " + str(err))
    else:
        return data

3. EAFP: easier to ask forgiveness

Python's idiom is to try the operation and catch the failure, rather than checking every precondition first. Try to open the file and catch FileNotFoundError, instead of checking existence and then opening — the check-then-act version has a race: the file can vanish between the two steps.

4. Raising useful errors

When your own code detects bad input, raise a specific exception with a message that says what was wrong and what was expected. Skillzify's flowchart parser raises ValueError with the offending line number, so a learner's broken code produces a helpful message instead of a crash. A good error message names the value that failed and the value that was expected, so the person reading it can fix the input without opening the source code.
lessons.task: Write load_scores as above, then test it against three files: a missing file, a file with broken JSON, and a valid file. Confirm each case behaves as intended, then write a version with a bare except and show why it hides a typo bug.
checks: Why catch FileNotFoundError instead of a bare except?
A bare except catches everything, including typos and interrupts, hiding real bugs. Catching the specific error keeps other failures visible.
What is EAFP and why does Python prefer it?
Easier to ask forgiveness than permission: try the operation and handle the failure. It avoids check-then-act races and reads more directly.
interview: What is the difference between except Exception and a bare except?
except Exception catches most errors but lets system-level ones like KeyboardInterrupt through; a bare except catches literally everything, including those.
What is the difference between else and finally in a try block?
else runs only when no exception occurred; finally runs always, for cleanup, whether or not an exception was raised.
